tiers.name: Beginner
tiers.blurb: The foundation exam. It checks that you know the ideas, words and rules of this course. Pass it and your course certificate is issued.

tiers.name: Intermediate
tiers.blurb: Numbers, comparisons and “which is right here?” questions. This exam checks that you can apply the ideas, not just recall them.

tiers.name: Hard
tiers.blurb: Client scenarios, grey areas and traps. This exam checks judgement: what you would actually say and do when it matters.

mf-foundations.hook: From SIPs to SEBI's 2026 rules: the ideas every fund conversation rests on.
fun: Industry AUM is a stock, not a flow: it moves with new money and with market prices, which is why a record AUM does not mean record investor returns.
A 50% fall needs a 100% gain to recover. That one line explains why chasing a silver rally can hurt so much.
traps: Treating AUM growth as investor returns.
Reading a quarter-end liquid fund outflow as retail panic.
Calling any market-linked product safe or guaranteed.

i.prompt: Industry AUM rises 4% in a month with net inflows of 0.5%. The rest of the rise most likely came from:
i.why: AUM change = net flows + market movement. If flows explain little, markets explain the rest.

i.prompt: A client says AUM grew 20% so every investor earned 20%. The best reply is:
options: "You're right, it is the same thing."
AUM is the same as NAV
It is only for debt funds
AUM growth includes new money, so it does not show what an investor earned
i.why: AUM mixes flows and market value. Investor return depends on the fund and the dates.

i.prompt: A headline says ₹1.8 lakh crore left mutual funds in March. First you should check:
i.why: Quarter-end debt outflows are usually corporate liquid fund movements, not retail panic.

i.prompt: Advance tax dates fall on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and:
i.why: These four dates drive corporate cash needs and liquid fund redemptions.

i.prompt: The underlying portfolio of a direct plan and a regular plan of the same scheme is:
i.why: Only the cost differs, because of the distributor commission.

i.prompt: Switching from a regular plan to a direct plan of the same scheme is:
options: A taxable transfer that may also carry exit load
i.why: It is treated as redemption and purchase.

i.prompt: The 2026 'true to label' rules aim to make sure:
options: A fund's portfolio matches its category name
i.why: The answer is “A fund's portfolio matches its category name”. Names must reflect what is held.

i.prompt: A cap on overlap between thematic and diversified funds makes thematic funds:
i.why: Distinct themes mean fewer common stocks, so more concentration, not less risk.

i.prompt: Two flexi cap funds give very different returns. The most likely reason is:
options: Different market-cap mix, sector weights and style
i.why: The category sets limits, the manager chooses within them.

i.prompt: A published fund return of 12% and your own return of 9% in the same fund may differ because:
options: Timing of your cash flows, plan type and taxes
i.why: Published returns assume a single lump sum on one date.

i.prompt: A client with a lump sum is anxious after a 13% fall. A practical middle path is:
options: Put it all in a sectoral fund
Keep it in a savings account forever
An STP from a liquid fund into equity
i.why: STP stages the entry and the money earns while waiting.

i.prompt: In a market fall, the most damaging client action is usually:
options: Stopping SIPs or redeeming at lows
i.why: Falls are normal. Acting on fear is what locks in loss.

i.prompt: Minimum investment for a SIF under SEBI's framework is:
i.why: SIFs sit between MFs and PMS with a ₹10 lakh minimum.

i.prompt: PMS trades differ from MF trades for tax because:
options: In PMS, each trade can be taxed in the client's hands
i.why: Securities in a PMS are in the client's name, so tax follows trades.

i.prompt: Equity fund units held for 15 months are taxed as:
options: Long-term, with gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year taxed at 12.5%
i.why: Over 12 months is long-term for equity funds.

i.prompt: A client with ₹3 lakh long-term equity gains in a year taxable base is roughly:
i.why: Only the portion above the annual exemption is taxed.

i.prompt: In large caps, passive funds often compete well because:
options: Many active funds struggle to beat the index after costs
i.why: Segments with efficient pricing reward low cost.

i.prompt: A 50% fall in silver needs what gain to recover?
i.why: The answer is “100%”. If 100 falls to 50, it must double.

i.prompt: Which phrase crosses the line into a promise?
options: "Historically, long periods have reduced the chance of loss."
"This fund will double your money in five years."
i.why: The answer is “"This fund will double your money in five years."”. 'Will' turns history into a guarantee.

i.prompt: Record SIP inflows in a falling month signal:
i.why: SIP flows during falls show investors staying the course.

h.prompt: A client sees 'Industry AUM down 10% in March' and wants to stop his SIP. Which reply is best?
options: "AUM falling means the fund is failing, so stop."
"Don't worry, it will recover by next month."
"AUM does not matter to you at all."
"AUM fell mainly because of market values, and SIP money kept coming in. Your plan is built for falls like this."
h.why: Break the headline into flows and prices, then connect to the plan, without a date promise.

h.prompt: A client wants only 'last year's best category'. The honest advice is:
options: Category flows show sentiment, not future returns, so tie the choice to his goal
h.why: Performance chasing is a common behaviour trap.

h.prompt: A fund's regular plan returns 11.2% and direct 11.9%. An investor asks why. You say:
options: The gap is the distribution cost, and the question is whether the advice is worth it to you
h.why: Identical portfolios, different cost. Be honest about the value of advice.

h.prompt: A distributor says 'The fund is 100% safe, SEBI regulated'. This is:
options: Misleading, because regulation does not remove market risk
h.why: No market-linked product can be called safe.

h.prompt: An investor in the 30% slab asks if he should switch a large equity holding to rebalance. First step:
options: Check the tax and exit load on the switch and use the annual exemption in stages
Redeem and wait for a dip
h.why: The answer is “Check the tax and exit load on the switch and use the annual exemption in stages”. Every switch is a taxable sale.

h.prompt: Client holds 6 equity funds with an overlap above 60%. Best advice:
options: Consolidate, because he owns much of one portfolio multiple times
h.why: Overlap hides the lack of diversification.

h.prompt: A 'thematic' fund held 60% of the same stocks as a diversified fund. Why did SEBI step in?
options: They beat the index too often
Investors thought they were diversifying but were not
h.why: Overlap reduced the value of having two funds.

h.prompt: An anxious client calls after a 12% fall. What should you do first?
options: Listen, give context, and reconnect to his goal
h.why: Context, plan and honesty prevent panic selling.

h.prompt: The client says 'I'll redeem now and re-enter when it settles'. The strongest point is:
options: You need to be right twice and recoveries often start before things feel settled
h.why: The answer is “You need to be right twice and recoveries often start before things feel settled”. Timing needs two correct calls.

h.prompt: A new investor wants a ₹5 crore PMS because the minimum is high and so 'it must be better'. You say:
options: Higher minimum does not mean better outcomes, so look at suitability and fees
h.why: Minimums are about structure, not skill.

h.prompt: A client wants silver because it jumped 100% last year. A responsible response is:
options: Size it small as a diversifier and explain the volatility
h.why: The answer is “Size it small as a diversifier and explain the volatility”. Don't chase last year's winners.

h.prompt: A colleague quotes 'category flows' as proof a theme will win. You respond:
options: Flows show what investors want, not what will perform
h.why: They indicate sentiment, which can reverse.

h.prompt: An investor's SIP is in a fund that lags peers for a year. Before switching, check:
options: Rolling returns, process and whether the style is out of favour
h.why: The answer is “Rolling returns, process and whether the style is out of favour”. One year of lag may be a style cycle.

h.prompt: A client in the highest slab wants a quick view on debt funds vs FD. A fair comparison needs:
options: Post-tax, post-inflation return and the time horizon
h.why: The answer is “Post-tax, post-inflation return and the time horizon”. Compare on the same after-tax basis.

h.prompt: Which is the worst way to pitch a SIP?
options: "If you invest every month for five years you will surely make money."
"SIP builds a habit and averages entry cost."
h.why: SIPs do not guarantee profit over any period.

h.prompt: A client says the fund's 3-year return is 14% but his statement shows 9%. Which action helps?
options: Tell him the fund is wrong
Calculate his XIRR and explain the timing of his instalments
h.why: The answer is “Calculate his XIRR and explain the timing of his instalments”. XIRR reflects his actual cash flows.

h.prompt: Which product choice shows suitability thinking?
options: Matching liquidity, horizon and risk before choosing the product
h.why: The answer is “Matching liquidity, horizon and risk before choosing the product”. Suitability comes before product.

h.prompt: A prospect wants a SIF for ₹8 lakh. The correct statement is:
options: The minimum for a SIF is ₹10 lakh, so it is not possible
SIF is the same as an MF
h.why: The answer is “The minimum for a SIF is ₹10 lakh, so it is not possible”. Minimum is ₹10 lakh per investor.

h.prompt: A client says silver is 'safe like gold'. Best correction:
options: Silver is far more volatile than gold, so size it smaller
h.why: Silver's market is smaller and has industrial demand.

h.prompt: When market falls are routine, a good proactive step is:
options: Call clients before they call you with context and their plan
h.why: Proactive calls prevent panic decisions.

regulation.hook: Who watches the watchers? Meet the sponsor, trustee, AMC, custodian, AMFI and SEBI, and learn what you may and may not say to clients.
fun: Your units sit in a trust, and the securities are held by a separate custodian. That split is deliberate protection.
'Direct' and 'regular' plans hold exactly the same portfolio. Only the cost differs.
traps: Promising a return, even softly.
Forgetting the ARN and EUIN on an application.
Mixing up what the riskometer shows (risk) with what it does not (returns).

i.prompt: Which body issues ARNs to mutual fund distributors?
i.why: The answer is “AMFI”. AMFI registers distributors.

i.prompt: The securities of a mutual fund are held by:
i.why: The answer is “The custodian”. Separation of duties.

i.prompt: The unit records of investors are kept by:
i.why: The answer is “The registrar and transfer agent”. RTA.

i.prompt: Who sets up the mutual fund trust?
i.why: The answer is “The sponsor”. Sponsor creates the trust.

i.prompt: A riskometer is updated:
options: Regularly, based on the scheme's holdings
i.why: The answer is “Regularly, based on the scheme's holdings”. Reflects current risk.

i.prompt: A large cap fund must keep at least what in large caps?
i.why: The answer is “80%”. SEBI category rule.

i.prompt: The expense ratio is shown in:
i.why: The answer is “The NAV, already deducted”. Deducted daily.

i.prompt: A direct plan has a lower expense ratio because it has no:
i.why: The answer is “Distributor commission”. Same portfolio.

i.prompt: Exit load applies when you:
i.why: The answer is “Redeem within the stated period”. Check the scheme document.

i.prompt: KYC for investing is:
options: Mandatory and valid across fund houses once done
i.why: The answer is “Mandatory and valid across fund houses once done”. One-time.

i.prompt: A nominee gets:
options: The units on the holder's death
i.why: The answer is “The units on the holder's death”. Smoother claims.

i.prompt: The standard risk disclosure says investments are:
i.why: The answer is “Subject to market risks”. Standard line.

i.prompt: Past performance disclaimers say it:
options: May or may not be sustained in future
i.why: The answer is “May or may not be sustained in future”. Standard.

i.prompt: Which complaint platform is run by SEBI?
i.why: The answer is “SCORES”. Online grievance system.

i.prompt: A complaint should first go to:
i.why: The answer is “The fund house”. Escalate later.

i.prompt: Joint holding 'either or survivor' means:
options: One holder can operate the folio
i.why: The answer is “One holder can operate the folio”. Choose the mode.

i.prompt: SEBI's categories exist so that:
options: Funds with the same label are comparable
i.why: The answer is “Funds with the same label are comparable”. Comparability.

i.prompt: The trustees:
options: Oversee the AMC for unit holders
i.why: The answer is “Oversee the AMC for unit holders”. Oversight.

i.prompt: Mis-selling includes:
options: Recommending a product for commission over suitability
i.why: The answer is “Recommending a product for commission over suitability”. Ethics.

i.prompt: A SEBI-registered distributor must show on forms:
i.why: The answer is “ARN and EUIN”. Identification.

h.prompt: A client asks 'Is my money safe if the AMC fails?' Best answer:
options: Assets sit in a trust with a custodian, but market risk remains
h.why: The answer is “Assets sit in a trust with a custodian, but market risk remains”. Be precise.

h.prompt: A distributor promises 12% to close a sale. This is:
h.why: The answer is “Mis-selling”. No guarantees.

h.prompt: A client wants to compare a small cap fund with a liquid fund. Your view:
options: Different categories carry different risk, so compare within category
h.why: The answer is “Different categories carry different risk, so compare within category”. Apples and oranges.

h.prompt: A client refuses to nominate. You:
options: Explain the family risk and ask again
h.why: The answer is “Explain the family risk and ask again”. Inform and document.

h.prompt: An investor says 'Direct is cheaper so advice is useless'. Fair reply:
options: Direct saves cost, and the question is whether advice is worth it
h.why: The answer is “Direct saves cost, and the question is whether advice is worth it”. Honest.

h.prompt: A client wants a refund of an exit load because he 'forgot'. Advice:
options: Explain the scheme document terms; loads apply by rule
h.why: The answer is “Explain the scheme document terms; loads apply by rule”. Rules.

h.prompt: A colleague uses an ad with last year's return only. Concern:
h.why: The answer is “Missing disclaimers and balance”. Rules on advertising.

h.prompt: An investor's complaint was ignored for a month. Next step:
h.why: The answer is “Escalate on SCORES”. Escalation path.

h.prompt: A client says 'riskometer is moderate so no loss'. You:
options: Riskometer shows risk level, not no-loss
h.why: The answer is “Riskometer shows risk level, not no-loss”. Understand.

h.prompt: Why record the client's goal and horizon?
options: Suitability and protection for both parties
h.why: The answer is “Suitability and protection for both parties”. Documentation.

h.prompt: A fund's name suggests 'safe' but it holds equity. Concern:
options: Names must reflect holdings, and risk must be disclosed
h.why: The answer is “Names must reflect holdings, and risk must be disclosed”. True to label.

h.prompt: A relative wants you to submit his KYC using your email. You:
options: Insist on the client's own contact details
h.why: The answer is “Insist on the client's own contact details”. Protect the client.

h.prompt: A client wants to give you his OTP. You:
h.why: The answer is “Refuse, as OTPs are personal”. Security.

h.prompt: A new SEBI circular changes a rule. You:
options: Read the update and apply it, noting the date
h.why: The answer is “Read the update and apply it, noting the date”. Stay current.

h.prompt: A client asks you to hide his ARN trail. You:
h.why: The answer is “Decline, transparency is required”. Ethics.

h.prompt: Who owns the units in a trust-based mutual fund?
options: The unit holders collectively through the scheme
h.why: The answer is “The unit holders collectively through the scheme”. Trust structure.

h.prompt: A friend asks for 'insider' fund news. You:
options: Decline and rely on public disclosures
h.why: The answer is “Decline and rely on public disclosures”. Ethics.

h.prompt: A client's address changed. Why update the folio?
options: To receive statements and verify changes
h.why: The answer is “To receive statements and verify changes”. Records.

h.prompt: A buyer claims 'SEBI approved so risk free'. You:
h.why: The answer is “Regulation sets rules, not outcomes”. Clarify.

h.prompt: An investor wants to know categories before buying. You:
options: Explain what each category must hold and the risk
h.why: The answer is “Explain what each category must hold and the risk”. Education.

financial-maths.hook: The arithmetic of money: compounding, CAGR, XIRR and the cost of costs, made friendly.
fun: At 12% a year money doubles in about 6 years, and doubles again in the next 6. The Rule of 72 does that in your head.
A 1% yearly cost gap on ₹10 lakh over 20 years costs about ₹16 lakh.
traps: Using CAGR for an SIP when XIRR is the right measure.
Ignoring inflation when setting a goal amount.
Treating absolute return as if time did not matter.

i.prompt: ₹1,00,000 grows at 8% a year for 3 years. The future value is about:
At 9% a year, money doubles in about how many years by the Rule of 72?
i.why: The answer is “8”. 72 ÷ 9 = 8.

i.prompt: A ₹1 lakh investment becomes ₹1.61 lakh in 5 years. The CAGR is about:
i.why: The answer is “10%”. 1.1⁵ = 1.61.

i.prompt: What is the present value of ₹1,21,000 due in 2 years at 10% a year?
i.why: The answer is “₹1,00,000”. Discount: 1,21,000 ÷ 1.21.

i.prompt: A 9% return with 5% inflation gives a real return of about:
A ₹10,000 monthly SIP at 12% a year for 10 years grows to about:
i.why: The lesson example gives about ₹23.2 lakh on ₹12 lakh invested.

i.prompt: A fall of 25% needs what gain to recover?
A fund with beta 1.2 may fall by how much if the market falls 10%?
i.why: The answer is “About 12%”. Beta scales the market move.

i.prompt: A bond fund with modified duration 4 may change by about how much if yields rise 0.5%?
i.why: Price change ≈ −duration × change in yield.

i.prompt: A goal costs ₹50 lakh today. With 6% inflation, in 10 years it costs about:
i.why: The answer is “₹89.5 lakh”. 50 × 1.06¹⁰ ≈ 89.5.

i.prompt: ₹1 lakh at 10% simple interest for 5 years becomes:
i.why: Simple interest adds 10% of the original each year.

i.prompt: Which measure suits a SIP with many cash flows?
i.why: The answer is “XIRR”. XIRR handles different dates.

i.prompt: 100% growth in 3 years versus 100% in 10 years: which has the higher CAGR?
i.why: Same total in less time means a higher yearly rate.

i.prompt: +50% then −50% leaves ₹100 at:
The gap between 12% and 11% over 20 years on ₹10 lakh is about:
i.why: The answer is “₹16 lakh”. ₹96 lakh vs ₹81 lakh.

i.prompt: Standard deviation measures:
options: How much returns swing around their average
i.why: The answer is “How much returns swing around their average”. Higher means a bumpier ride.

i.prompt: Maximum drawdown shows:
i.why: The answer is “The largest peak-to-trough fall”. It is the worst pain a holder felt.

i.prompt: ₹2,00,000 at 12% for 2 years becomes:
A step-up SIP differs from a flat SIP because it:
i.why: The answer is “Raises the instalment each year”. The contribution grows with income.

i.prompt: Lump sum often beats SIP in:
i.why: The answer is “Rising markets over long periods”. More money is invested earlier.

h.prompt: A client's SIP shows 11% XIRR while the fund's 3-year return is 14%. Both are correct because:
options: XIRR reflects his own cash flow dates
h.why: The timing of instalments changes the personal return.

h.prompt: A client says 12% gives 120% in 10 years. The correct number is about:
h.why: The answer is “210%”. 1.12¹⁰ = 3.1, a 210% gain.

h.prompt: A 7% FD with 6% inflation and 30% tax: the real after-tax return is about:
h.why: After tax, 4.9% minus 6% inflation is negative.

h.prompt: Which goal needs the lowest return assumption?
options: A house deposit needed in 2 years
h.why: Short goals need steadier, lower assumptions.

h.prompt: For a ₹50 lakh goal in 10 years at 12%, why not assume 15%?
options: An optimistic assumption can leave the goal short
h.why: Plans should be built on cautious assumptions.

h.prompt: Two funds average 12% but fund A is steadier. After 10 years, who ends richer?
options: Fund A, because volatility drags the compound return
h.why: The answer is “Fund A, because volatility drags the compound return”. Volatility reduces compound growth.

h.prompt: Why is lump sum vs SIP often wrongly debated?
options: Most people have monthly income and cannot invest a lump sum they do not have
h.why: The practical choice depends on cash flow.

h.prompt: An advisor shows return as 'absolute 80%' for a 7-year fund. A better presentation is:
h.why: The answer is “CAGR over the period”. CAGR annualises the growth.

h.prompt: A fund has the highest return but a 55% drawdown. The client needs money in 3 years. You say:
options: The drawdown risk may not fit a 3-year horizon
h.why: The answer is “The drawdown risk may not fit a 3-year horizon”. Risk numbers matter for short horizons.

h.prompt: A client compares an ELSS lump sum in March to SIPs. You mention:
options: Each SIP instalment has its own lock-in and entry price
h.why: The answer is “Each SIP instalment has its own lock-in and entry price”. Lock-in is per purchase.

h.prompt: For XIRR, which cash flow sign convention applies?
options: Investments negative, withdrawals and final value positive
h.why: The answer is “Investments negative, withdrawals and final value positive”. Money out of pocket is negative.

h.prompt: A client claims 'costs of 1% don't matter'. The best answer is:
options: Over 20 years it can cost a large slice of the final corpus
h.why: The answer is “Over 20 years it can cost a large slice of the final corpus”. Costs compound against you.

h.prompt: You want to compare a fund with its category using one number over time. Best:
options: Rolling returns or CAGR over the same period
h.why: The answer is “Rolling returns or CAGR over the same period”. Same period, same measure.

h.prompt: A parent needs ₹40 lakh in 10 years for education inflating at 8%. Today's equivalent need is:
options: Higher, about ₹86 lakh in future money
h.why: 40 × 1.08¹⁰ ≈ 86 if ₹40 lakh is today's cost.

h.prompt: Why can a 100% gain over 3 years look better than it is?
h.why: The answer is “It ignores the time taken”. Absolute returns hide time.

h.prompt: An investor has a ₹10 lakh lump sum and a nervous temperament. A suitable plan is:
options: All at once at the highest risk
Hold all in cash for 10 years
Stage it over months, accepting that it may lag a rally
h.why: Behaviour decides whether the plan is followed.

h.prompt: A fund 'beat' the benchmark by 1% but with a beta of 1.4. This suggests:
options: The excess may just be extra risk
h.why: The answer is “The excess may just be extra risk”. Beta shows higher market risk.

h.prompt: Which statement about the Rule of 72 is correct?
options: It is a quick estimate, best near 6-10% rates
h.why: The answer is “It is a quick estimate, best near 6-10% rates”. It gives approximate doubling time.

h.prompt: A ₹5,000 SIP started at age 25 vs ₹10,000 at 35, same return, retirement at 60. Who has the larger corpus likely?
options: The one who started at 25, due to compounding time
h.why: The answer is “The one who started at 25, due to compounding time”. Time often beats a larger amount.

h.prompt: An advisor ignores inflation in a retirement plan. The result will be:
options: A corpus that looks adequate but buys less
h.why: The answer is “A corpus that looks adequate but buys less”. Inflation erodes purchasing power.

sip-planning.hook: SIP, STP, SWP: the three letters that run most client portfolios, and how to use each for the right goal.
fun: Rupee-cost averaging does not remove risk. It removes the need to guess the right day.
Most SIP failures are not market failures: they are bounced mandates and stopped instalments.
traps: Pausing an SIP because of fear.
Using an STP to chase returns instead of to stage entry.
Withdrawing too much too early from a retirement SWP.

i.prompt: In an SIP, a lower NAV gives:
i.why: The answer is “More units”. Fixed money.

i.prompt: SIP returns are best measured with:
i.why: The answer is “XIRR”. Cash flows.

i.prompt: A step-up SIP:
i.why: The answer is “Raises the instalment over time”. Growth with income.

i.prompt: STP stands for:
i.why: The answer is “Systematic Transfer Plan”. Moves money.

i.prompt: SWP stands for:
i.why: The answer is “Systematic Withdrawal Plan”. Regular redemption.

i.prompt: In SWP, tax applies to:
options: The gain part of each withdrawal
i.why: The answer is “The gain part of each withdrawal”. Gain portion.

i.prompt: Sequence risk is:
i.why: The answer is “Early poor returns while withdrawing”. Order of returns.

i.prompt: A safe waiting place for an STP lump sum is:
options: A liquid or short duration fund
i.why: The answer is “A liquid or short duration fund”. Parking.

i.prompt: A short goal under 3 years suits:
i.why: The answer is “Low-risk funds”. Horizon.

i.prompt: A goal's target should be adjusted for:
i.why: The answer is “Inflation”. Future cost.

i.prompt: A good SIP date is:
i.why: The answer is “A few days after salary”. Avoid bounces.

i.prompt: A bounced SIP is caused by:
i.why: The answer is “Insufficient bank balance”. Mandate.

i.prompt: An emergency fund helps by:
i.why: The answer is “Preventing forced SIP stops”. Resilience.

i.prompt: The best way to invest is:
options: The one the client can follow
i.why: The answer is “The one the client can follow”. Behaviour.

i.prompt: Over many years, SIP gains come mainly from:
i.why: The answer is “The fund's returns”. SIP is a method.

i.prompt: A 10% yearly step-up on ₹10,000 means year-2 instalment of:
Which option reduces regret for a nervous lump-sum investor?
i.why: The answer is “STP over months”. Staged entry.

i.prompt: A buffer of 1-2 years of withdrawals is held in:
i.why: The answer is “Lower-risk funds”. Sequence protection.

i.prompt: Which statement about SIPs is false?
i.why: The answer is “They guarantee profit”. False.

i.prompt: Rupee-cost averaging means:
options: Buying more units when prices are low
i.why: The answer is “Buying more units when prices are low”. Mechanism.

h.prompt: The market is down 15% and a client wants to pause SIP. You say:
options: The same amount buys more units now, so staying is usually wise if the goal is far
h.why: The answer is “The same amount buys more units now, so staying is usually wise if the goal is far”. Behaviour.

h.prompt: A client has ₹30 lakh from property. A sensible approach:
h.why: The answer is “STP into equity over 6-12 months”. Process.

h.prompt: A retiree wants ₹50,000 a month from ₹1 crore. You warn:
options: 6% withdrawal may drain it in a bad sequence
h.why: The answer is “6% withdrawal may drain it in a bad sequence”. Sequence risk.

h.prompt: A client says his SIP failed twice. You:
options: Move the date after salary and keep a buffer
h.why: The answer is “Move the date after salary and keep a buffer”. Fix cause.

h.prompt: A parent wants ₹50 lakh for college in 12 years. First step:
options: Inflate the goal to future rupees
h.why: The answer is “Inflate the goal to future rupees”. Goal maths.

h.prompt: A client's income rises 10% a year. Best SIP structure:
h.why: The answer is “Step-up SIP”. Match income.

h.prompt: A 28-year-old wants to stop SIP to buy a phone. You:
options: Discuss priorities and a pause rather than a stop
h.why: The answer is “Discuss priorities and a pause rather than a stop”. Discipline.

h.prompt: For a goal in 2 years, which fund is suitable?
h.why: The answer is “Short duration or liquid”. Horizon.

h.prompt: A client says SIP 'guarantees profit if long enough'. You:
h.why: The answer is “No method guarantees profit”. Honesty.

h.prompt: The client wants to switch SIP funds monthly to chase the best. You:
options: Explain costs, tax and behaviour risk
h.why: The answer is “Explain costs, tax and behaviour risk”. Discipline.

h.prompt: An investor has no emergency fund. Priority:
h.why: The answer is “Build it before long-term SIPs”. Order.

h.prompt: A goal portfolio near its date should:
h.why: The answer is “Move gradually to safer funds”. De-risk.

h.prompt: What is the best test of an STP?
options: Does the client stick to the plan?
h.why: The answer is “Does the client stick to the plan?”. Behaviour.

h.prompt: An SWP from equity funds in a crash. Risk:
h.why: The answer is “Selling units cheaply”. Sequence.

h.prompt: A client wants to compare SIP return with FD return. Use:
h.why: The answer is “XIRR vs post-tax FD return”. Like-for-like.

h.prompt: A client sets SIP step-up 30% a year on a modest income. Issue:
options: Unsustainable and may lead to missed instalments
h.why: The answer is “Unsustainable and may lead to missed instalments”. Realistic.

h.prompt: An SIP is in a fund that lagged for a year. Before stopping:
h.why: The answer is “Check rolling returns and process”. Don't react.

h.prompt: Goal maths needs:
options: Amount, date, inflation and return assumption
h.why: The answer is “Amount, date, inflation and return assumption”. Inputs.

h.prompt: A client asks to invest the lump sum on the 'best day'. You:
options: Explain no one times it, and offer staged entry
h.why: The answer is “Explain no one times it, and offer staged entry”. No timing.

h.prompt: Which is a sign of a healthy SIP plan?
options: Reviewed yearly with goal and amount
h.why: The answer is “Reviewed yearly with goal and amount”. Process.

equity-funds.hook: Large, mid, small, flexi, ELSS, sectoral, value: the equity menu, explained so you can order with confidence.
fun: Under AMFI's list, the top 100 companies by market value are large caps. Companies drift between buckets as prices move.
A multi cap fund must hold at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps.
traps: Comparing funds from different categories.
Buying a theme after it has already run.
Thinking ELSS reduces market risk because it saves tax.

i.prompt: Which are large caps under AMFI's list?
i.why: The answer is “Top 100 by market cap”. Ladder.

i.prompt: A mid cap fund must keep at least what in mid caps?
i.why: The answer is “65%”. SEBI rule.

i.prompt: A multi cap fund must hold at least what in each segment?
i.why: The answer is “25%”. SEBI rule.

i.prompt: A focused fund holds at most:
i.why: The answer is “30 stocks”. Concentration.

i.prompt: ELSS lock-in is:
i.why: The answer is “3 years”. 80C option.

i.prompt: An ELSS must invest at least what in equity?
i.why: The answer is “80%”. SEBI rule.

i.prompt: A sectoral fund holds at least what in its sector?
i.why: The answer is “80%”. Narrow bet.

i.prompt: A value or contra fund must hold at least what in equity?
i.why: The answer is “65%”. Style funds.

i.prompt: Companies move between market-cap buckets because:
i.why: The answer is “Their market values change”. Prices move.

i.prompt: The best way to judge a fund over time is:
i.why: The answer is “Rolling returns within its category”. Consistency.

i.prompt: Which fund has most freedom to shift between large, mid and small caps?
i.why: The answer is “Flexi cap”. No minimums.

i.prompt: A dividend yield fund is:
options: An equity fund with market risk
i.why: The answer is “An equity fund with market risk”. Dividend does not remove risk.

i.prompt: An ELSS under the new tax regime gives:
i.why: The answer is “No 80C deduction”. Regime matters.

i.prompt: A typical satellite holding is:
i.why: The answer is “A thematic fund”. Narrow bets.

i.prompt: Overlap between funds means:
i.why: The answer is “Common stocks held by both”. Hidden duplication.

i.prompt: Value investing buys stocks that look:
i.why: The answer is “Cheap versus fundamentals”. Style.

i.prompt: Contra funds bet on:
i.why: The answer is “Out-of-favour stocks”. Against the crowd.

i.prompt: Large size can hurt which funds most?
i.why: The answer is “Mid and small cap funds”. Liquidity.

i.prompt: Which is a sound first step to pick an equity fund?
i.why: The answer is “Decide goal and horizon”. Order of decisions.

i.prompt: Small caps tend to:
i.why: The answer is “Fall harder in downturns”. Higher risk.

h.prompt: A client wants only small caps because they gave the highest return last year. You say:
options: Size them as one part of the portfolio, as falls can be deep
h.why: The answer is “Size them as one part of the portfolio, as falls can be deep”. Chasing.

h.prompt: A client wants one fund for 10 years. A balanced suggestion:
options: A flexi cap as a core, reviewed yearly
h.why: The answer is “A flexi cap as a core, reviewed yearly”. Core idea.

h.prompt: It is March and a client wants ELSS in a hurry. You first ask:
options: Which tax regime he is on
h.why: The answer is “Which tax regime he is on”. Regime check.

h.prompt: A value fund has trailed for three years. Before selling, check:
options: Whether it is following its process and the style is out of favour
h.why: The answer is “Whether it is following its process and the style is out of favour”. Style cycles.

h.prompt: A client holds 12 funds. You:
options: Check overlap and consolidate to a few with different jobs
h.why: The answer is “Check overlap and consolidate to a few with different jobs”. Simplify.

h.prompt: A fund suddenly holds 50% mid caps in a large cap category. Concern:
h.why: The answer is “Style drift against the label”. True to label.

h.prompt: A client says 'defence is hot, move 50%'. A sensible view:
options: Keep themes small and agree review rules
h.why: The answer is “Keep themes small and agree review rules”. Satellite.

h.prompt: A mid cap fund's AUM has tripled. A relevant point:
options: Size can limit nimbleness in mid-sized stocks
h.why: The answer is “Size can limit nimbleness in mid-sized stocks”. Liquidity.

h.prompt: A focused fund underperforms due to one stock. Lesson:
h.why: The answer is “Concentration raises single-stock risk”. Few stocks.

h.prompt: A client in the old regime has ₹1.5 lakh 80C already used by EPF. ELSS:
options: Adds no extra deduction in that case
h.why: The answer is “Adds no extra deduction in that case”. Limit.

h.prompt: A client wants a dividend yield fund for 'safe income'. You say:
options: Dividend stocks can still fall and payouts vary
h.why: The answer is “Dividend stocks can still fall and payouts vary”. Don't assume.

h.prompt: An NFO claims a 'new theme'. Check:
options: Whether it duplicates existing funds with long records
h.why: The answer is “Whether it duplicates existing funds with long records”. Don't be dazzled.

h.prompt: A multi cap fund and flexi cap fund differ because:
options: Multi cap has minimum 25% in each segment
h.why: The answer is “Multi cap has minimum 25% in each segment”. Rules.

h.prompt: A client says 'the fund's NAV is ₹15 so cheap'. Reply:
h.why: The answer is “NAV does not show value”. Myth.

h.prompt: An investor is nervous about a 40% fall in small caps. You:
options: Reset size to what he can hold through
h.why: The answer is “Reset size to what he can hold through”. Fit risk.

h.prompt: To compare two large cap funds, the best is:
options: Rolling returns, downside capture, cost, concentration
h.why: The answer is “Rolling returns, downside capture, cost, concentration”. Multi-factor.

h.prompt: A client wants to buy the top 1-year fund. You say:
options: Past winners often rotate, so check fit and consistency
h.why: The answer is “Past winners often rotate, so check fit and consistency”. Recency.

h.prompt: A client asks if sectoral funds can be core. You say:
options: Usually no, they are too concentrated
h.why: The answer is “Usually no, they are too concentrated”. Satellite.

h.prompt: A client in his 60s asks for 100% small cap. You:
options: Explain the risk and advise a balanced allocation
h.why: The answer is “Explain the risk and advise a balanced allocation”. Suitability.

h.prompt: How often should you review fund choices?
h.why: The answer is “At least yearly”. Review.

economy-markets.hook: The big picture behind every fund: growth, rates, inflation, flows and valuation.
fun: Private consumption is roughly 58% of India's GDP: the biggest engine.
Domestic SIP money now gives institutions around ₹32,000 crore a month to deploy, which cushions falls when foreign investors sell.
traps: Assuming strong GDP means markets cannot fall.
Forgetting that real return = nominal return − inflation.
Reading a rate hike as a crash signal.

i.prompt: India's real GDP growth in FY26 (provisional) was:
i.why: The course data shows 7.7% vs 7.1% in FY25.

i.prompt: Private consumption is about what share of GDP?
i.why: The answer is “About 58%”. It is the largest driver of growth.

i.prompt: After GST rationalisation in Sep 2025, mainly how many slabs remained?
i.why: Simplification cut prices on many daily-use goods.

i.prompt: RBI's repo rate after the October 2026 hike is:
i.why: The answer is “5.50%”. It was a 25 bps hike from 5.25%.

i.prompt: RBI's CPI target is:
i.why: The inflation target is 4% with a tolerance band.

i.prompt: A rate hike generally hurts which funds the most?
i.why: The answer is “Long-duration bond funds”. Long bonds fall most when yields rise.

i.prompt: A 6.5% FD in a 5% inflation year earns a real return of about:
i.why: The answer is “1.5%”. Nominal minus inflation, before tax.

i.prompt: Which ministry spending takes about 14.7% of central spending in FY27?
i.why: The answer is “Defence”. ₹7.85 lakh crore of ~₹53.5 lakh crore.

i.prompt: High crude prices tend to:
i.why: The answer is “Widen the current account deficit”. India imports most of its crude.

i.prompt: In 2025 domestic institutions' ownership of NSE-listed companies:
options: Overtook FPIs' for the first time in over two decades
i.why: The answer is “Overtook FPIs' for the first time in over two decades”. SIP flows have made DIIs the anchor.

i.prompt: Roughly how much do SIP flows give DIIs to deploy each month?
i.why: The course states about ₹32,000 crore a month.

i.prompt: The earnings yield is:
i.why: It can be compared with the 10-year G-sec yield.

i.prompt: PEG ratio equals:
i.why: The answer is “P/E ÷ growth”. It adjusts the P/E for growth.

i.prompt: The largest sector in the Nifty 50 is:
i.why: The answer is “Financial services”. Roughly a third of the index.

i.prompt: Which scheme rewards incremental manufacturing in electronics, pharma and autos?
i.why: The answer is “PLI”. Production Linked Incentive.

i.prompt: AMFI releases monthly mutual fund data around the:
i.why: It is a routine date on the data calendar.

i.prompt: The RBI's MPC meets how many times a year?
i.why: The answer is “Six”. Six scheduled meetings.

i.prompt: A stronger dollar and higher US yields tend to:
options: Pull FPI money out of emerging markets
i.why: Capital flows go to higher yields and a strong dollar.

i.prompt: Households shifting from FDs, gold and property into financial assets is called:
i.why: MF AUM has grown faster than bank deposits.

i.prompt: What does a high P/E imply for a company growing slowly?
i.why: High P/E is only defensible with high durable growth.

h.prompt: A client says the October rate hike means the market will crash. A balanced reply is:
options: It is normalisation after a cut cycle, so review debt duration, not the equity plan
h.why: The answer is “It is normalisation after a cut cycle, so review debt duration, not the equity plan”. Link the move to the plan, calmly.

h.prompt: Rates just rose. Which debt move is most sensible for a one-year goal?
h.why: Shorter duration reduces mark-to-market loss.

h.prompt: A client uses a 7% FD as the benchmark for all returns. You point out:
options: Real, post-tax return can be near zero
h.why: The answer is “Real, post-tax return can be near zero”. Compare after tax and inflation.

h.prompt: FPIs sold heavily but the market fell little. The likely explanation is:
options: DII and SIP buying cushioned the fall
h.why: The answer is “DII and SIP buying cushioned the fall”. Domestic flows have become an anchor.

h.prompt: A client says 'GDP is strong so the market can't fall'. Correct response:
options: Markets can fall even when GDP is strong because prices reflect expectations and valuations
h.why: Valuations and flows matter in the short run.

h.prompt: An RM wants to explain why banks matter so much for large-cap funds. Use:
options: Financial services are about a third of the Nifty 50
h.why: Large-cap funds therefore own big private banks.

h.prompt: Which indicator would you check before a client meeting about inflation?
h.why: The answer is “The monthly CPI release”. CPI is released around the 12th.

h.prompt: A client asks whether to buy a rate-sensitive sector after a hike. A careful answer:
options: Realty and autos can feel pressure, so size cautiously
h.why: Rate-sensitive sectors can be pressured.

h.prompt: Which line best frames a macro story for clients?
options: Growth strong, rates normalising, domestic flows anchoring the market
h.why: The answer is “Growth strong, rates normalising, domestic flows anchoring the market”. A balanced story builds trust.

h.prompt: A client wants to time equity entry around the budget. A fair point:
options: Budgets matter for sectors and capex, but timing short-term moves is unreliable
h.why: The answer is “Budgets matter for sectors and capex, but timing short-term moves is unreliable”. Use budgets for themes, not timing.

h.prompt: The rupee weakens and crude rises. Who is hurt most?
options: Oil importers and companies with imported inputs
h.why: A weak rupee and costly crude raise input costs.

h.prompt: A forecast says inflation could hit 5% in FY27. A client's FD pays 6.5%. The real return is:
h.why: The answer is “About 1.5% before tax”. Nominal minus inflation, before tax.

h.prompt: A client sees DII ownership above FPI and concludes risk is zero. You say:
options: It cushions falls but does not remove them
h.why: The answer is “It cushions falls but does not remove them”. Domestic flows can also slow.

h.prompt: Why do government capex and private capex often move together?
options: Public spending can crowd in private investment
h.why: The answer is “Public spending can crowd in private investment”. Capex creates demand and confidence.

h.prompt: When valuations are stretched, a client should:
options: Look at growth durability and earnings yield versus bonds
h.why: Valuation literacy guards against paying too much.

h.prompt: A client asks if India will pass Japan in dollar GDP. The honest reply:
options: It depends on growth and the rupee, so there is no certainty
h.why: The answer is “It depends on growth and the rupee, so there is no certainty”. Rupee moves affect dollar GDP.

h.prompt: What is the best proof that Indian households are saving differently?
options: MF AUM growing faster than bank deposits
h.why: The answer is “MF AUM growing faster than bank deposits”. Financialisation of savings.

h.prompt: A senior citizen worries about hikes. Which statement is balanced?
options: Hikes can hurt long-duration funds but raise future accrual
h.why: Mark-to-market loss, higher future yield.

h.prompt: A client asks about tariffs. The RBI has flagged them as:
options: A reason to expect lower prices
A key growth risk through trade uncertainty
h.why: Global trade uncertainty weighs on growth.

h.prompt: Which sentence is a good use of macro data with clients?
options: "Here is one fact and what it means for your plan."
h.why: The answer is “"Here is one fact and what it means for your plan."”. Short, relevant and tied to the plan.

hybrid-funds.hook: Equity, debt and everything in between: how hybrid funds balance risk, and how each is taxed.
fun: Arbitrage funds are hedged, yet taxed like equity funds if at least 65% sits in equity-related instruments.
Balanced advantage funds shift equity with valuations, so they can lag in a strong rally.
traps: Assuming 'hybrid' means 'safe'.
Forgetting the 65% equity line for tax.
Holding several hybrids that overlap.

i.prompt: Aggressive hybrid equity range is:
i.why: The answer is “65-80%”. Category.

i.prompt: Conservative hybrid equity range is:
i.why: The answer is “10-25%”. Category.

i.prompt: An arbitrage fund holds at least what in equity-related instruments?
i.why: The answer is “65%”. For equity taxation.

i.prompt: Arbitrage funds earn from:
i.why: The answer is “Cash-futures price gap”. Hedged.

i.prompt: Balanced advantage funds adjust equity based on:
i.why: The answer is “Valuations”. Models.

i.prompt: Equity savings funds hold:
i.why: The answer is “Equity, arbitrage and debt”. Mix.

i.prompt: A multi asset fund holds at least how many asset classes?
i.why: The answer is “Three”. With 10% each.

i.prompt: A fund with at least 65% equity is taxed as:
i.why: The answer is “Equity”. The line.

i.prompt: LTCG on equity above the exemption is taxed at:
i.why: The answer is “12.5%”. As in the course.

i.prompt: STCG on equity is taxed at:
i.why: The answer is “20%”. As in the course.

i.prompt: An arbitrage fund suits:
i.why: The answer is “Short-term parking with equity taxation”. Stable returns.

i.prompt: A balanced advantage fund may lag in:
i.why: The answer is “Strong rallies”. Holds back at high valuations.

i.prompt: A conservative hybrid is likely taxed:
i.why: The answer is “At slab rate”. Mostly debt.

i.prompt: Why may arbitrage returns dip?
i.why: The answer is “Futures premium narrows”. Spread.

i.prompt: Hybrid funds suit investors wanting:
i.why: The answer is “Some equity with cushioned falls”. Mix.

i.prompt: A good first step to choose a hybrid is:
options: Decide how much fall the client can handle
i.why: The answer is “Decide how much fall the client can handle”. Fit.

i.prompt: Multi asset funds usually add:
i.why: The answer is “Gold or silver”. Third engine.

i.prompt: Net equity in a BAF can differ from gross equity because of:
i.why: The answer is “Hedging with futures”. Hedge.

i.prompt: Stacking several similar hybrids mainly gives:
i.why: The answer is “Overlap”. Duplication.

i.prompt: Equity savings funds are taxed as equity when:
options: 65% is in equity and arbitrage together
i.why: The answer is “65% is in equity and arbitrage together”. Threshold.

h.prompt: A client needs money in 10 months and has ₹20 lakh idle. Hybrid choice:
options: Arbitrage fund as a short-term parking, with FD-like expectations
h.why: The answer is “Arbitrage fund as a short-term parking, with FD-like expectations”. Horizon.

h.prompt: A client believes BAF 'cannot fall'. You:
options: BAF can fall, only usually less in sharp equity falls
h.why: The answer is “BAF can fall, only usually less in sharp equity falls”. Honest.

h.prompt: A 70-year-old wants better than FD with small falls. You:
options: Consider conservative hybrid or equity savings with realistic expectations
h.why: The answer is “Consider conservative hybrid or equity savings with realistic expectations”. Suitability.

h.prompt: A client holds an aggressive hybrid and a flexi cap. Check:
h.why: The answer is “Overlap in equity exposure”. Duplication.

h.prompt: A client wants to rebalance equity and debt himself every quarter. You note:
options: Tax and exit load on each switch, compared with a hybrid's internal rebalancing
h.why: The answer is “Tax and exit load on each switch, compared with a hybrid's internal rebalancing”. Tax.

h.prompt: A client asks why BAF lagged in a strong rally. You say:
options: The model reduced equity as valuations rose
h.why: The answer is “The model reduced equity as valuations rose”. Design.

h.prompt: A fund's name says 'equity savings' but equity+arbitrage is 50%. Tax:
h.why: The answer is “Likely not equity-taxed”. Threshold.

h.prompt: A client says 'arbitrage gives 14%'. You:
options: Returns track short rates, so expect modest numbers
h.why: The answer is “Returns track short rates, so expect modest numbers”. Honest.

h.prompt: A first-time investor asks for a hybrid. You:
options: Start gentle and add pure equity later
h.why: The answer is “Start gentle and add pure equity later”. Behaviour.

h.prompt: A multi asset fund and a BAF both claim 'smooth'. Compare:
options: Mix, gold role, model and drawdowns
h.why: The answer is “Mix, gold role, model and drawdowns”. Details.

h.prompt: Why is the tax status important when picking arbitrage over liquid?
options: Equity-taxed gains may suit high-slab investors
h.why: The answer is “Equity-taxed gains may suit high-slab investors”. Tax matters.

h.prompt: A client says 'conservative hybrid has no equity risk'. You:
options: It holds 10-25% equity, so small falls are possible
h.why: The answer is “It holds 10-25% equity, so small falls are possible”. Know the mix.

h.prompt: A client wants to put emergency money into a BAF. You:
options: Prefer liquid funds for emergency needs
h.why: The answer is “Prefer liquid funds for emergency needs”. Liquidity.

h.prompt: A client compares aggressive hybrid with large cap. Difference:
h.why: The answer is “Hybrid holds 20-35% debt, cushioning falls”. Mix.

h.prompt: A BAF model shows high equity after a fall. This reflects:
h.why: The answer is “Cheaper valuations raising equity allocation”. Dynamic.

h.prompt: The best test for hybrid suitability is:
options: Can the client hold through the fund's worst fall?
h.why: The answer is “Can the client hold through the fund's worst fall?”. Behaviour.

h.prompt: A client with 15-year horizon only buys conservative hybrid. Risk:
options: Returns may not beat inflation enough for the goal
h.why: The answer is “Returns may not beat inflation enough for the goal”. Under-risking.

h.prompt: A hybrid manager hedges equity with futures. The effect is:
options: Net equity falls while gross equity stays
h.why: The answer is “Net equity falls while gross equity stays”. Hedge.

h.prompt: The 65% line matters because:
h.why: The answer is “It decides tax treatment”. Tax.

h.prompt: A client asks to hold arbitrage for 5 years for growth. You:
options: Explain it is parking, not growth
h.why: The answer is “Explain it is parking, not growth”. Role.

passive-etf.hook: Index funds, ETFs, tracking error and smart beta: how to own the market cheaply and honestly.
fun: An ETF trades on the exchange all day, while an index fund is bought at the day's NAV.
Passive does not mean safe: an index fund falls fully with its index.
traps: Ignoring the bid-ask spread on an ETF.
Comparing funds on different indices.
Chasing last year's best smart-beta factor.

i.prompt: A passive fund aims to:
options: Beat the index by a lot
i.why: The answer is “Match an index”. Replication.

i.prompt: An ETF is traded on:
i.why: The answer is “The stock exchange”. Intraday.

i.prompt: ETFs require:
i.why: The answer is “A demat account”. Demat.

i.prompt: Tracking difference is:
i.why: The answer is “Fund return minus index return”. Gap.

i.prompt: Tracking error is:
i.why: The answer is “How much the gap wiggles”. Volatility of the gap.

i.prompt: Which usually explains most tracking difference?
i.why: The answer is “The expense ratio”. Costs.

i.prompt: Smart beta funds follow:
i.why: The answer is “A rule-based index”. Factors.

i.prompt: Which index is broad and covers 500 companies?
i.why: The answer is “Nifty 500”. Breadth.

i.prompt: A cheap fund in a falling market will:
i.why: The answer is “Fall with its index”. Risk.

i.prompt: Active management tends to find more room in:
i.why: The answer is “Small caps”. Less efficient.

i.prompt: An index fund is bought at:
i.why: The answer is “The day's NAV”. NAV.

i.prompt: For SIP, easiest is:
i.why: The answer is “Index fund”. Auto-debit.

i.prompt: The bid-ask spread is:
options: The cost of trading an ETF
i.why: The answer is “The cost of trading an ETF”. Hidden cost.

i.prompt: iNAV is:
options: Indicative NAV of an ETF during the day
i.why: The answer is “Indicative NAV of an ETF during the day”. Reference value.

i.prompt: A fund tracking Nifty Next 50 holds:
options: The next 50 large companies after Nifty 50
i.why: The answer is “The next 50 large companies after Nifty 50”. Index choice.

i.prompt: Rebalancing a core portfolio happens when:
options: The mix drifts far from plan
i.why: The answer is “The mix drifts far from plan”. Control.

i.prompt: A factor index based on 'momentum' holds:
i.why: The answer is “Stocks with recent strength”. Factor.

i.prompt: Passive investing does not mean:
i.why: The answer is “Safe”. Risk remains.

i.prompt: Small ETF with low volume may have:
i.why: The answer is “Wide spread”. Liquidity.

i.prompt: Comparing funds on the same index, check:
i.why: The answer is “Expense ratio and tracking difference”. Cost and tracking.

h.prompt: A client says index funds can't lose. You:
h.why: The answer is “They fall with the index”. Honest.

h.prompt: A client wants an ETF but has no demat. You:
h.why: The answer is “Suggest an index fund”. Wrapper.

h.prompt: Two Nifty 50 funds differ 0.3% yearly. The likely cause:
h.why: The answer is “Expense ratio and tracking”. Cost.

h.prompt: A client wants momentum funds after 40% return. You:
options: Explain factor cycles, and size small
h.why: The answer is “Explain factor cycles, and size small”. Chasing.

h.prompt: A client prefers one-fund simplicity. A passive core:
options: Broad index fund plus growth fund
h.why: The answer is “Broad index fund plus growth fund”. Simplicity.

h.prompt: An ETF trades at a premium to iNAV. Advice:
options: Avoid overpaying and use limit orders
h.why: The answer is “Avoid overpaying and use limit orders”. Execution.

h.prompt: Why can active add value in small caps but less in large caps?
h.why: The answer is “Large caps are heavily researched”. Efficiency.

h.prompt: A client wants to sell an index fund after a 15% fall. You:
options: Remind him of the plan and horizon
h.why: The answer is “Remind him of the plan and horizon”. Behaviour.

h.prompt: An index fund has high tracking error. Concern:
options: It may not follow its index well
h.why: The answer is “It may not follow its index well”. Quality.

h.prompt: A client asks 'Is a new index fund better?'
options: Check cost, size and tracking, not age alone
h.why: The answer is “Check cost, size and tracking, not age alone”. Evidence.

h.prompt: A client mixes Nifty 50 and Nifty 100 index funds. Concern:
h.why: The answer is “Heavy overlap”. Overlap.

h.prompt: A client wants to hold only passive. A balanced view:
options: Fine for core, consider active in less efficient areas
h.why: The answer is “Fine for core, consider active in less efficient areas”. Mix.

h.prompt: A smart beta fund underperforms for 3 years. Lesson:
h.why: The answer is “Factors go through cycles”. Cycles.

h.prompt: An investor says 'ETF cost is zero'. You:
h.why: The answer is “Remember expense ratio and spread”. Costs.

h.prompt: A client wants a fund that 'beats the index'. For a passive fund:
h.why: The answer is “That is not its aim”. Purpose.

h.prompt: A client compares a Nifty 50 ETF and Nifty 500 index fund. Difference:
h.why: The answer is “Breadth and risk”. Index choice.

h.prompt: Which portfolio is more diversified?
options: A broad index fund covering many sectors
h.why: The answer is “A broad index fund covering many sectors”. Diversification.

h.prompt: A client wants a gold ETF and Nifty ETF in one account. You:
h.why: The answer is “Explain each role and size”. Roles.

h.prompt: Why check fund size for an index fund?
options: Very small funds may be shut or track poorly

behaviour.hook: Why smart people make poor money decisions, and how to be the voice that keeps clients in their seat.

Promising a rebound date.
Letting a hot theme set the plan.

i.why: The answer is “Fixate on the purchase price”. Bias.

stock-basics.hook: Own a slice of a business, buy it from a stranger in a millisecond, and know exactly who protects you. This is how the machine works.
fun: India settles share trades the next working day (T+1), among the fastest cycles of any major market.
A share you cannot sell is only a number: liquidity, the ease of finding a buyer, matters as much as price.
traps: Thinking a stop-loss order guarantees the exit price.
Treating an IPO as a guaranteed listing gain.
Believing a stock split or bonus issue makes you richer.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A share is a unit of ownership in a company. A shareholder owns a small part of the business and shares in its profits and risks.
i.why: Share: A share is a unit of ownership in a company. A shareholder owns a small part of the business and shares in its profits and risks.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? The bid is the highest price a buyer offers and the ask is the lowest price a seller wants. The gap between them is a hidden cost of trading.
i.why: Bid-ask spread: The bid is the highest price a buyer offers and the ask is the lowest price a seller wants. The gap between them is a hidden cost of trading.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade listed shares at transparent prices. India’s main exchanges are NSE and BSE.
i.why: Stock exchange: A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade listed shares at transparent prices. India’s main exchanges are NSE and BSE.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Dividend” is correct?
options: Every company must pay a dividend every year.
A dividend is a share of profit a company pays to shareholders, usually per share. The board decides it and it is not guaranteed.
A split doubles the value of your holding.
A stock exchange fixes the price of every share by decree.
i.why: Correct: A dividend is a share of profit a company pays to shareholders, usually per share. The board decides it and it is not guaranteed. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which statement about “IPO” is correct?
options: Every IPO lists at a profit, so applying is risk-free.
An initial public offering is when a company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money, and then lists on an exchange.
A trading account stores your shares permanently.
The spread is a tax collected by the government on every trade.
i.why: Correct: An initial public offering is when a company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money, and then lists on an exchange. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A stop-loss order triggers a sale when the price falls to a level you set, to cap the loss on a position. In a fast fall it may fill below that level.
i.why: Stop-loss order: A stop-loss order triggers a sale when the price falls to a level you set, to cap the loss on a position. In a fast fall it may fill below that level.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Nifty 50” is correct?
options: The Nifty 50 is a single company’s share you can buy on the exchange.
A limit order always executes immediately at the best available price.
The Nifty 50 is an index of 50 large companies listed on the NSE. It tracks the market’s direction but cannot be bought directly.
A trading account stores your shares permanently.
i.why: Correct: The Nifty 50 is an index of 50 large companies listed on the NSE. It tracks the market’s direction but cannot be bought directly. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Price band” is correct?
options: A price band limits how far a share can rise or fall in one day. When it is hit, trading in that share is halted or restricted for the day.
A price band guarantees a share can never lose more than the band in total.
A limit order always executes immediately at the best available price.
A broker guarantees profits on the trades they execute for you.
i.why: Correct: A price band limits how far a share can rise or fall in one day. When it is hit, trading in that share is halted or restricted for the day. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A demat account holds your shares in electronic form, like a bank account holds money. The depositories NSDL and CDSL keep the records.
i.why: Demat account: A demat account holds your shares in electronic form, like a bank account holds money. The depositories NSDL and CDSL keep the records.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A limit order buys or sells only at your chosen price or better. It may not execute if the market never reaches that price.
i.why: Limit order: A limit order buys or sells only at your chosen price or better. It may not execute if the market never reaches that price.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? India settles most share trades one working day after the trade: shares and money change hands on the next working day.
i.why: T+1 settlement: India settles most share trades one working day after the trade: shares and money change hands on the next working day.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A trading account is the account through which you place buy and sell orders. It connects your bank account and your demat account.
i.why: Trading account: A trading account is the account through which you place buy and sell orders. It connects your bank account and your demat account.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Intraday trade” is correct?
options: Intraday trading is a safe way to invest because nothing is held overnight.
Bonus shares are free money that raise your wealth immediately.
Every company must pay a dividend every year.
An intraday trade is opened and closed on the same day, so no shares are delivered. Profit or loss is the difference in price.
i.why: Correct: An intraday trade is opened and closed on the same day, so no shares are delivered. Profit or loss is the difference in price. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Diversification” is correct?
options: Diversification guarantees that you will never lose money.
Every IPO lists at a profit, so applying is risk-free.
Diversification spreads money across many shares, sectors or assets so that one failure does not sink the whole portfolio.
The spread is a tax collected by the government on every trade.
i.why: Correct: Diversification spreads money across many shares, sectors or assets so that one failure does not sink the whole portfolio. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? SEBI is India’s securities market regulator. It protects investors, registers intermediaries and writes the rules for exchanges and brokers.
i.why: SEBI: SEBI is India’s securities market regulator. It protects investors, registers intermediaries and writes the rules for exchanges and brokers.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Delivery trade” is correct?
options: Delivery trades must be sold before the market closes on the same day.
A broker guarantees profits on the trades they execute for you.
A split doubles the value of your holding.
In a delivery trade you take the shares into your demat account and can hold them for as long as you like.
i.why: Correct: In a delivery trade you take the shares into your demat account and can hold them for as long as you like. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Market capitalisation” is correct?
options: Market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by the number of shares issued. It is the market’s value of the whole company.
Market capitalisation is the total cash a company holds in its bank accounts.
A stock exchange fixes the price of every share by decree.
Delivery trades must be sold before the market closes on the same day.
i.why: Correct: Market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by the number of shares issued. It is the market’s value of the whole company. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Bonus issue” is correct?
options: Bonus shares are free money that raise your wealth immediately.
Delivery trades must be sold before the market closes on the same day.
A bonus issue gives existing shareholders extra shares free, out of the company’s reserves. The price adjusts down, so total value stays about the same.
Every company must pay a dividend every year.
i.why: Correct: A bonus issue gives existing shareholders extra shares free, out of the company’s reserves. The price adjusts down, so total value stays about the same. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

i.prompt: Which term is described here? A stockbroker is a registered intermediary who places your buy and sell orders on the exchange and charges brokerage for the service.
i.why: Stockbroker: A stockbroker is a registered intermediary who places your buy and sell orders on the exchange and charges brokerage for the service.

i.prompt: Which statement about “Stock split” is correct?
options: A split doubles the value of your holding.
A stock split divides each share into more shares at a lower price. The number of shares rises but the total value you own is unchanged.
Every IPO lists at a profit, so applying is risk-free.
A limit order always executes immediately at the best available price.
i.why: Correct: A stock split divides each share into more shares at a lower price. The number of shares rises but the total value you own is unchanged. The other statements are common misunderstandings.

h.prompt: Which of these statements is NOT correct?
options: Intraday trading is a safe way to invest because nothing is held overnight.
SEBI is India’s securities market regulator. It protects investors, registers intermediaries and writes the rules for exchanges and brokers.

h.prompt: Nikhil bought at ₹200 and sets an instruction to sell if the price drops to ₹180. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Stop-loss order. A stop-loss order triggers a sale when the price falls to a level you set, to cap the loss on a position. In a fast fall it may fill below that level.

Diversification guarantees that you will never lose money.

h.prompt: Shares bought on Monday are credited to the buyer’s demat account on Tuesday. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is T+1 settlement. India settles most share trades one working day after the trade: shares and money change hands on the next working day.

h.prompt: Kabir logs in to place a buy order that debits his bank and delivers shares to his locker. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Trading account. A trading account is the account through which you place buy and sell orders. It connects your bank account and your demat account.

h.prompt: A share shows ₹100.00 for sellers to hit and ₹100.40 for buyers to pay at the same moment. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Bid-ask spread. The bid is the highest price a buyer offers and the ask is the lowest price a seller wants. The gap between them is a hidden cost of trading.

h.prompt: A company has 100 crore shares trading at ₹50 each, valuing the business at ₹5,000 crore. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Market capitalisation. Market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by the number of shares issued. It is the market’s value of the whole company.

h.prompt: A private company invites ordinary investors to apply for its first-ever shares before it lists. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is IPO. An initial public offering is when a company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money, and then lists on an exchange.

h.why: That statement is a common misunderstanding. The accurate version: The Nifty 50 is an index of 50 large companies listed on the NSE. It tracks the market’s direction but cannot be bought directly.

h.prompt: A stock reaches its daily upper limit and no buyer can push it higher that day. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Price band. A price band limits how far a share can rise or fall in one day. When it is hit, trading in that share is halted or restricted for the day.

h.prompt: Meena’s purchased shares are stored electronically in her name, with no paper certificates. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Demat account. A demat account holds your shares in electronic form, like a bank account holds money. The depositories NSDL and CDSL keep the records.

h.prompt: Asha buys 10 units of a listed company and now owns a tiny slice of its business. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Share. A share is a unit of ownership in a company. A shareholder owns a small part of the business and shares in its profits and risks.

h.prompt: A company pays ₹5 per share out of its profits to everyone on its register. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Dividend. A dividend is a share of profit a company pays to shareholders, usually per share. The board decides it and it is not guaranteed.

h.prompt: Ravi uses a registered app-based intermediary to place orders on the exchange for a small fee on each trade. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Stockbroker. A stockbroker is a registered intermediary who places your buy and sell orders on the exchange and charges brokerage for the service.

h.prompt: A broker is found misusing client funds and the market regulator steps in to penalise it. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is SEBI. SEBI is India’s securities market regulator. It protects investors, registers intermediaries and writes the rules for exchanges and brokers.

h.prompt: Buy and sell orders from thousands of investors are matched on a regulated electronic platform. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Stock exchange. A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade listed shares at transparent prices. India’s main exchanges are NSE and BSE.

h.prompt: Priya wants to buy at ₹500 or lower and will wait rather than pay ₹510. Which idea does this show?
h.why: This is Limit order. A limit order buys or sells only at your chosen price or better. It may not execute if the market never reaches that price.
